note: Append-only. Ids are permanent: a case that no longer applies gets `retired` with a reason and keeps its number. Coverage is a CLAIM; scripts/case-registry.ts turns it into evidence by executing it.

cases.title: Prototype pollution through a request-supplied key
cases.rationale: A value the caller controls is used directly as a computed key on a write. Setting `__proto__` re-parents the object, which is the whole of CWE-1321. This is the shortest form the bug takes in real code.

cases.title: Prototype pollution through an unguarded merge helper
cases.rationale: `for (const k in src) dst[k] = src[k]` over a caller-supplied source is the shape behind the published prototype-pollution advisories in the deep-merge family. The key is never named in the source, so no allowlist can be read off the file.
cases.code: function merge(dst, src) { for (const k in src) { dst[k] = src[k]; } return dst; }

cases.title: A computed write onto `this` inside a class method
cases.rationale: Reads like noise and is not. Verified by execution: calling the method with `__proto__` re-parents the instance. Registered so the finding cannot be dismissed as an FP a second time.
cases.code: class Bag { set(k, v) { this[k] = v; } }

cases.title: Array append written as a self-indexed length
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `arr.length` is a number, so the key cannot name a prototype slot. Written with `arr` as a PARAMETER on purpose: a locally-constructed array was already cleared by an older path, so `const arr = []` would pass whether or not the fix exists — a case that cannot fail is not evidence.

cases.title: A key iterated from a const array of string literals
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. Every value the key can take is written out in the same file and none is a dangerous property, so the question is decidable rather than assumed. An author who lists `__proto__` themselves still gets the report.
cases.code: const KEYS = ["alpha", "beta"]; const o = {}; for (const k of KEYS) { o[k] = 1; }

cases.title: A copy loop over an object the module itself owns
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. Nothing an attacker supplies reaches the loop. eslint-plugin-security reports this twice, once per side of the assignment; the noise is by their design, not a disagreement about the facts.
cases.code: const cfg = { a: 1 }; const out = {}; for (const k in cfg) { out[k] = cfg[k]; }

cases.title: A merge helper guarded by Object.hasOwn
cases.rationale: NOT a defect — it is the documented remediation for ILB-0002. Reporting the fix leaves the user with nothing to do, which is how a rule teaches people to disable it.
cases.code: function merge(dst, src) { for (const k in src) { if (Object.hasOwn(src, k)) dst[k] = src[k]; } }

cases.title: A timing-unsafe comparison of a bearer token
cases.rationale: `===` on a secret short-circuits at the first differing byte, so response time leaks the shared prefix. Observed guarding five HTTP endpoints in a real deployment.
cases.code:
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
function check(req, secret) { if (req.headers.authorization === secret) { return true; } return false; }

cases.title: An AST discriminant compared with ===
cases.rationale: NOT a defect. `node.kind === SyntaxKind.X` is a tag comparison, not a secret. Eleven findings in the wild came from this one shape before it was sealed.
cases.code:
import ts from 'typescript';
function f(node) { return node.kind === ts.SyntaxKind.ClassDeclaration; }

cases.title: Prototype pollution through a key reached by a call
cases.rationale: The key is computed at runtime by a function this file cannot summarise. Registered as an OPEN question rather than a claim: whether an unresolvable key should report is the same judgement as FP-010, and no rule currently answers it deliberately.

cases.title: execFile with a caller-chosen argument
cases.rationale: Written as a decoy on the assumption that no shell means no defect. Executed: `execFileSync('echo', ['safe; echo PWNED'])` yields the literal string, so command injection is indeed impossible — but the caller still chooses an ARGUMENT, and a leading `-` is a flag. The rule reports CWE-88 argument injection here, not CWE-78, and goes silent once `--` terminates option parsing. The rule was right and the case was wrong.

const cp = require('child_process');
function f(req) { cp.execFile('ls', [req.query.dir]); }

cases.title: Cross-document message broadcast to any origin
cases.rationale: `'*'` tells the browser to deliver the message to whatever document currently occupies the frame. If the frame has navigated, or was navigated by an attacker, the payload lands in their document. MDN names this the primary security concern of the API.

cases.title: A concrete target origin
cases.rationale: The same call with an origin the browser must match before delivering. Looks identical in shape to the defect and must stay quiet — this is the form the fix takes.

cases.title: A wildcard string that is not a target origin
cases.rationale: `'*'` appearing as the message BODY rather than the origin argument. A rule matching the literal without regard to argument position reports this.

cases.title: Request object spread straight into a Mongo filter
cases.rationale: A caller-controlled object becomes the query document. `{"$ne": null}` as a password turns the lookup into 'any user', which is the canonical NoSQL authentication bypass. Missed until 2026-08-30: the rule early-returned on any first argument that was not an object literal, so the most direct form of the bug went unreported.
cases.code:
import { MongoClient } from 'mongodb';
async function f(db, req) { return db.collection('u').find(req.body); }

cases.title: The same lookup with the value pinned to a string
cases.rationale: Coercing to a primitive removes the operator surface entirely. The fix, and it must stay quiet.
cases.code:
import { MongoClient } from 'mongodb';
async function f(db, req) { return db.collection('u').find({ name: String(req.body.name) }); }

cases.title: A module-scope constant reported as user input
cases.rationale: An object built from a `const` string in the same file. Nothing here is caller-controlled. Reported until 2026-08-30 with the message `User input "NAME" is used directly`, because any bare identifier in a filter counted as user input. That one heuristic produced this false positive and the miss in ILB-0121 together.

cases.title: A vendor secret key committed as a literal
cases.rationale: `sk_live_` is Stripe's published prefix for a live secret key. The name of the binding is irrelevant — the FORMAT is somebody else's contract, so the finding does not depend on what a project calls its variables.

cases.title: The same key read from the environment
cases.rationale: The literal is gone; the name is unchanged. A rule keying on the NAME still reports this, which is the false positive the format check exists to avoid.

cases.title: A publishable key, which is meant to be in the bundle
cases.rationale: `pk_live_` is the half Stripe documents as safe to ship to a browser. Reporting it teaches consumers to disable the rule.

cases.title: Nested quantifier over an overlapping character class
cases.rationale: `(a+)+$` is the textbook catastrophic backtrack: the inner and outer quantifiers can partition the same input exponentially many ways, so a non-matching string of length n costs 2^n steps.

cases.title: The same intent written without nesting
cases.rationale: One quantifier over one class matches the same language in linear time.

cases.title: Nested quantifiers over DISJOINT classes
cases.rationale: `(a+b+)+` nests, but the classes cannot overlap, so there is only one way to partition any input and no backtracking explosion. A rule matching the SHAPE rather than the ambiguity reports it.

cases.title: A reactive value missing from the dependency array
cases.rationale: The effect closes over `userId` and declares no dependency on it, so it keeps the value from the render in which it first ran. React's own docs call this the stale-closure bug; the symptom is a screen that silently shows another user's data after navigation.
cases.code:
import { useEffect } from 'react';
export function C({ userId }) { useEffect(() => { load(userId); }, []); return null; }

cases.title: The same effect with the value declared
cases.rationale: Adding the dependency is the whole fix, and it must stay quiet.
cases.code:
import { useEffect } from 'react';
export function C({ userId }) { useEffect(() => { load(userId); }, [userId]); return null; }

cases.title: A ref read inside an effect that declares nothing
cases.rationale: `useRef` returns a stable object, so React explicitly tells you NOT to list it. A rule treating every closed-over binding as reactive reports this, and reporting it teaches consumers to add a dependency React documents as wrong.
cases.code:
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
export function C() { const r = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { look(r.current); }, []); return null; }

cases.title: Model output written straight into the DOM
cases.rationale: A model's text is attacker-influenced whenever any part of the prompt is. Writing it to `innerHTML` makes prompt injection into stored XSS — OWASP's LLM02 in its shortest form.
cases.code:
import { generateText } from 'ai';
async function f(el, prompt) { const { text } = await generateText({ model: m, prompt }); el.innerHTML = text; }

cases.title: The same output assigned as text
cases.rationale: `textContent` cannot introduce markup. The fix, and it must stay quiet.
cases.code:
import { generateText } from 'ai';
async function f(el, prompt) { const { text } = await generateText({ model: m, prompt }); el.textContent = text; }

cases.title: A local string written to innerHTML in a file that also calls a model
cases.rationale: The sink is real but the value never touched the model. A rule keying on 'this file imports the AI SDK and something reaches innerHTML' reports it.
cases.code:
import { generateText } from 'ai';
async function f(el) { const label = 'Loading…'; el.innerHTML = label; }

cases.title: Two modules importing each other
cases.rationale: `a` imports `b`, `b` imports `a`. At runtime one of them observes the other half-initialised, so a `const` is `undefined` at module-evaluation time and the failure appears far from its cause. Needs real files: a cycle is a property of the module GRAPH, so a single source string cannot express one — the fixture pair under benchmarks/cases/fixtures/cycle exists for that reason.
cases.code:
import { b } from './b';
export const a = b;

cases.title: The same import, to a module that imports nothing back
cases.rationale: Structurally identical at the import site — same syntax, same directory, same resolver work. Only the far end differs, which is what makes it the decoy: a rule that reports on 'this file imports a sibling' rather than on the graph reports this too.
cases.code:
import { leaf } from './leaf';
export const a = leaf;

cases.title: Allocation sized by a request, on a handler whose parameter is not spelled req
cases.rationale: `Buffer.allocUnsafe(capacity)` where `capacity` comes from `req.query.capacity`. The rule recognised the request by the root identifier's SPELLING, against REQUEST_ROOTS = ['req','request','ctx','event'], so the identical handler written `(inbound, outbound)` — or TypeScript's own `(request: Request, response: Response)` renamed on the way in — allocated from a peer-chosen size and reported nothing. The rename probe found 18 true positives that went silent this way, with `.query.capacity` still in plain sight one link up. Fixed 2026-08-30 by asking readsRequestShape before walking to the root.

cases.title: A log line named message reported as bytes off the wire
cases.rationale: WIRE_NAMES hardcoded ['chunk','chunks','buffer','buf','payload','frame','packet','raw','message','msg'] with no way for a consumer to disagree. A project whose `message` is a log line, or whose `raw` is a template string, was reported on the word alone and could do nothing about it — an additive option can grow the list but never remove the word we guessed wrong about. Fixed 2026-08-30 by making wireNames, requestRootNames and countNames REPLACE their defaults; `wireNames: []` turns the name arm off entirely.
